tagline.en: A museum-style atlas of western Pennsylvania and the Mahoning Valley edge — steel, neighbors, sports, music, and cross-border history from Buhl Park.

title.en: West Pennsylvania & East Ohio history expert

greeting.en: Welcome. I am David — a regional historian for western Pennsylvania and eastern Ohio. We begin at Buhl Park, then read steel, Amish roads, Friday-night lights, music, and the Youngstown corridor just across the state line.

en.heroKicker: Regional history gallery · Mercer, Lawrence & Mahoning
en.heroLine: A scholastic atlas centered on Buhl Park — steel philanthropy, Amish neighbors, sports, music, and the Youngstown–Mahoning story just across the Ohio line.

en.storyModeCopy: Guided HyperFrames reel in a memorial-wall tone — timed scenes, optional narration (Google TTS). Runs once; Escape stops.

copy.en: Context: The Beaver and Erie Canal — also called the Erie Extension Canal — ran about 136 miles from the Ohio River at Beaver to Lake Erie at Erie (Beaver, Shenango, and Conneaut divisions). Roughly 137 locks climbed nearly 977 feet. Construction spanned the 1830s; the full line opened in 1844, linking Great Lakes trade to the Ohio–Mississippi system. Evidence: Sharpsville’s Lock No. 10 is widely cited as the only surviving lock — boats left Shenango slackwater into the canal channel (~7-foot lift). Lock 10 opened with a Greenville stretch about 1840. Canal towns (Sharon, Sharpsville, Clarksville, Big Bend) boomed until the Erie & Pittsburgh Railroad paralleled the route; after bankruptcy (~1870) the railroad abandoned the waterway (~1871–73, Elk Creek aqueduct collapse as pretext). Remnants remain near Shenango River Lake; Greenville Canal Museum and the Shenango Trail mark the old towpath.

narration.en: Chapter one — canal iron. Before Farrell’s mill and Buhl’s free green, boats climbed toward Lake Erie on the Erie Extension Canal. One hundred thirty-six miles, more than a hundred locks. Sharpsville’s Lock Ten is the stone that survived. Stand there and you are reading the valley before steel was king.

copy.en: Context: Christian H. Buhl founded Sharon Iron Works; his son Frank H. Buhl (1848–1918, Yale) clerked, managed, then controlled the works. Evidence: Buhl Steel Company organized in Sharon in 1896 with Frank as first president; open hearth 1897; absorbed by National Steel (1898) into the Carnegie orbit. With John Stevenson Jr. he broke ground for Sharon Steel Works / Sharon Steel Company in South Sharon in February 1900; sold about 1902 and retired into philanthropy (towns of Buhl, Minnesota and Buhl, Idaho carry his name). South Sharon — platted on undeveloped land — earned the nickname Magic City and was renamed Farrell in 1912 after James A. Farrell of U.S. Steel. Late 1920s: U.S. Steel valley plants plus Sharon Steel Hoop employed around ten thousand. Sharon Steel Corporation (from Sharon Steel Hoop, 1936) filed bankruptcy in 1987 and again in 1992 when the big Farrell mill closed; later Caparo, Duferco, and NLMK Pennsylvania kept steel operations on parts of the footprint. Buhl Mansion (1891, East State Street, Sharon) is on the National Register.

narration.en: Chapter two — steel. Frank Buhl’s Buhl Steel in eighteen ninety-six, then South Sharon’s mill in nineteen hundred — the Magic City that became Farrell. Ten thousand jobs at the peak. Bankruptcies closed the big mill in nineteen ninety-two, yet steel still works parts of that ground. Remember this map when you open Youngstown — same belt, same decade of loss.

copy.en: Context: Childless couple Frank and Julia (Forker) Buhl turned steel fortune into civic gifts — hospital, club, armory, annual Buhl Day. He preferred “farm” to “park” so no one would expect ticket booths and midways. Evidence: Between 1907 and 1911 he bought seven parcels in Hickory Township (now Hermitage), about 262.66 acres at assembly; later totals with Thornton Farm changes are often cited near 270–300 acres. Cleveland architect Charles W. Hopkinson and landscape architect George Rettig shaped the grounds; W. H. Way of Mayfield Country Club laid out the nine-hole course about 1914. Lake Julia (named for Julia), Casino ballroom (not gambling), bandstand, about ten tennis courts, athletic field with roughly a thousand-seat grandstand, and free golf. Construction spend about $385,000 (1911–15); deeded to the F.H. Buhl Trustees on 1 November 1915 for $1.00 plus endowment — facilities “forever free” for public recreation. The park still claims the nation’s only free public nine-hole golf course. Atlas hub: every spoke radiates from here.

narration.en: Chapter three — the gift. Frank and Julia Buhl bought the farm acres, built Lake Julia and the Casino, and deeded it all in nineteen fifteen for one dollar — forever free. Working families without a gate fee. Free golf still. Every pin on this atlas radiates from Buhl Farm Park.

copy.en: Context: Western Pennsylvania Old Order settlement — often called the Lawrence County or Byler Amish — clustered around New Wilmington and Volant in northern Lawrence and southern Mercer counties, not Lancaster. Conservative dress; burnt-orange or brown buggy tops noted in GAMEO and local reporting; Mifflin County roots and later Holmes County, Ohio ties. Evidence: Christian Yoder purchased land 1 April 1847; Abraham Zook 8 May 1847; Beiler/Byler families followed; Lawrence County organized 1849. An 1877 county history already counted Amish/Omish Mennonite settlers from Mifflin County. Later growth reached multi-district community size (roughly two thousand people and many one-room schools in late-twentieth-century reporting). Etiquette: neighbors, not exhibits — slow for buggies, buy when stands are open, photograph fields and towns, never faces or private yards without permission. About ten miles from Buhl Park.

narration.en: Chapter four — neighbors. Since eighteen forty-seven, Mifflin County families have farmed around New Wilmington — western Pennsylvania Amish country, not Lancaster. Brown-topped buggies, living districts. Share the lane. Keep cameras off people. Courtesy is the wall text.

copy.en: Context: Twin-city sports culture on the same mill labor market — Sharon Tigers versus Farrell Steelers in PIAA District 10. Football’s Steel Bowl is the named rivalry; boys’ basketball gym nights are equally storied. Evidence: Local press still counts Steel Bowl meetings across decades (including coverage of a seventy-second game); annual play paused roughly 2014–2021 then resumed. Sharon Tiger Stadium and Farrell venues (including later Paulekas / Pegues complex reporting) host the brand. Farrell’s Steelers nickname echoes mill identity. Buhl Farm’s original program already included a football field with grandstand seating and free golf — sport as civic gift before modern scoreboard nights.

narration.en: Chapter five — Friday lights. Sharon Tigers, Farrell Steelers, the Steel Bowl. Rival towns, shared valley. Buhl’s free fields and grandstand came first — then the stadium and gym nights that still fill the calendar.

copy.en: Context: Local airwaves and stages plus two national careers from Mercer County geography — different towns — and a related live-music corridor across the Ohio line in Youngstown. Evidence: WPIC signed on in 1938; mid-century hops, Marjon Records (polka and local sides), Apollo Maennerchor (German singing society tradition from 1870), Hermitage’s Menagerie, and free Buhl summer concerts fill the middle register. Sharon’s Anthony “Tony” Butala (born 20 November 1940) co-founded The Lettermen (1958); first Top Forty hit “The Way You Look Tonight” (1961); retired performing about 2019; group Walk of Fame star 2020. He opened a Vocal Group Hall of Fame museum in Sharon about 1998 (98 East State) — treat later foundation/relocation struggles as hometown project history, not a permanent tourist claim. Mercer borough’s Trent Reznor — Mercer High jazz band, circulating 1982 sax solo — founded Nine Inch Nails after leaving for Cleveland: same county, not a Sharon childhood claim. Related across the line: Cedars Lounge became a downtown Youngstown rock room in 1975 at 23 North Hazel under Tommy Simon; after a 2012 eviction the family reopened as Cedars West End at 706 Steel Street (2013). On the same downtown block, the State Theater ran as the Tomorrow Club (~1973) then Youngstown Agora (1978–82) — the big Federal Street rock hall a short walk from Cedars. Keep the towns straight on the map.

narration.en: Chapter six — music. Tony Butala took Sharon harmony to the nation with The Lettermen. Trent Reznor took Mercer High jazz band to industrial rock. Across the line, Cedars on Hazel and the Tomorrow Club — later the Agora — kept Youngstown rock alive downtown. Keep the geography honest.

copy.en: Context: Youngstown sits between Cleveland and Pittsburgh, about fifteen to twenty minutes from Sharon–Farrell, with no resident Cosa Nostra family — so both cities’ factions contested “the bug” (numbers), vending, and related rackets. The Saturday Evening Post’s March 1963 “Crime Town U.S.A.” fixed a media label. Evidence — rackets: mid-to-late 1970s Cleveland-aligned Carabbia brothers (“the Crabs”) versus Pittsburgh-aligned Jimmy Prato, Joey Naples, and Lenny Strollo; Cleveland boss John Scalish died 1976; Danny Greene car-bombed 6 October 1977 (Ronnie Carabbia among those convicted); Youngstown faction war peaking about 1978–1981; Charlie Carabbia disappeared December 1980 (Strollo later testified Prato and Naples ordered the killing). Evidence — steel, same decade: Black Monday, 19 September 1977 — Youngstown Sheet & Tube announced Campbell Works shutdown; about five thousand jobs gone at once; within about five years roughly fifty thousand Mahoning Valley jobs lost; U.S. Steel Ohio Works closed 1979. Ecumenical Coalition worker–community buyout failed after federal loan guarantees were withdrawn. 1990s FBI/RICO and Strollo cooperation are the legal coda, not the 1970s climax. Museum rules: Context versus Evidence; no private addresses; no true-crime tourism.

narration.en: Chapter seven — across the line. Youngstown’s big decade is the nineteen-seventies: Crime Town already printed, then Cleveland against Pittsburgh for the bug, Charlie Carabbia vanishing, and Black Monday — September nineteenth, nineteen seventy-seven — when Sheet and Tube closed Campbell Works. Same commute belt as Sharon and Farrell. Read the cards as a museum wall.

copy.en: Context: The atlas is present tense. Buhl Farm’s trust and partners still fund free golf, concerts, and trails on roughly two hundred seventy acres; Amish roads still need courtesy; Farrell’s steel footprint and Youngstown’s post–Black Monday landscape still shape work and memory across a porous state line. Evidence of care: slow for buggies; support valley tables when you can; treat organized-crime history as published record and court testimony — never rumor, never romanticized violence, never private addresses. The hub remains Buhl Farm Park because the Shenango Valley still meets there.

narration.en: Closing chapter — living valley. Keep Buhl free. Share Amish roads. Read Youngstown with Evidence, not rumor. The map still centers on the green Frank Buhl gave away.

South Sharon mill town — Magic City — renamed Farrell 1912. Sharon Steel Works from 1900; peak employment era ~10,000 valley workers; big mill closed 1992; later NLMK footprint.
1891 Richardsonian Romanesque home of Frank H. Buhl — Gilded Age steel wealth on the National Register.
Old Order / Lawrence County Amish from Mifflin County ~1847 — brown-topped buggies, living farms. Roughly ten miles from Buhl Park. Not Lancaster.
Small-town gateway to Amish-country shops and roadside stands — buy when open, photograph fields not people.
Home of Sharon Tigers football since the WPA era. Tradition from 1899; site of Steel Bowl clashes with Farrell.
Farrell Steelers boys basketball — District 10 powerhouse nicknamed for the mill town. Rivalry nights with Sharon still pack the gym.

Opened March 1974 in a former service station — motor-themed wings and a Sharon landmark after the steel peak.
Official site: serving the Shenango Valley from Stambaugh Avenue — authentic pizza, sandwiches, wings, and a casual pub. Claims over 70 years as one of America's older pizza shops. Call 724-347-3323.
Shenango Valley pizza institution since 1955 — neighborhood loyalty near Buhl Park.
Mahoning County seat — civic core minutes from Sharon–Farrell. Geography for 1970s rackets war and Black Monday steel collapse.
Youngstown Sheet & Tube corridor — Campbell Works closed Black Monday 19 Sept 1977 (~5,000 jobs). Industrial geography tied to Farrell/Sharon.
The state line between Mercer County, Pennsylvania, and Trumbull–Mahoning, Ohio. Same commute belt; different courts and newspapers — and historically different vice markets.
Working-class Mahoning suburbs southeast of Youngstown where period reporting placed Cleveland-aligned card and dice games. Minutes from the PA line — same commute belt as Sharon–Farrell.

Mahoning County mill suburb later tied in federal cases to large illegal gambling operations. Geography for the Pittsburgh-aligned Youngstown faction’s later cash businesses — Evidence belongs to the court record, not rumor.

tagline.en: Sharon Iron → Buhl Steel → park endowment

history.en: Evidence: Frank H. Buhl (1848–1918) organized Buhl Steel in Sharon in 1896, then with John Stevenson Jr. opened Sharon Steel Works in South Sharon in 1900 — the boom that made Farrell. His 1891 mansion on East State Street is on the National Register. Context: after selling about 1902 he poured fortune into civic gifts culminating in Buhl Farm Park.

Evidence: South Sharon sprang up on undeveloped land after the 1900 mill groundbreaking — the Magic City — and was renamed Farrell in 1912. Late-1920s valley plants employed around ten thousand. Sharon Steel’s 1987 and 1992 bankruptcies closed the big mill; Caparo, Duferco, and later NLMK kept steel on parts of the footprint.

Evidence: Sharpsville Lock No. 10 is cited as the only surviving lock of the Erie Extension (Beaver and Erie) Canal — ~7-foot lift from Shenango slackwater. Context: the 136-mile canal opened 1844 and was abandoned after rail competition in the early 1870s.

Families from Mifflin County — Zook, Byler, and others — settled farms around New Wilmington in the late 1840s. GAMEO and county histories place this among Pennsylvania's major western settlements. Distinctive brown or burnt-orange buggy tops mark the roads. Treat it as a living community, not Lancaster tourism copy.

Share the road with buggies, keep cameras on barns and fields — never people without clear permission — and buy from roadside stands when open. Sacred singing (Ausbund slow-tunes) is worship, not a soundtrack for visitors.
Volant sits on the approach to Amish farmland — shops, markets, and quiet roads. Use it as a respectful gateway from the Shenango Valley map, not as a private-farm pin drop.

The original farm park included a football field with a thousand-seat grandstand, tennis courts, and a nine-hole course laid out so anyone could play free. That free golf course still claims uniqueness in the United States. Recreation was Buhl's answer to steel-town life.

Evidence: Sharon Tigers football tradition dates to 1899; Tiger Stadium is remembered as a WPA-era home. Context: Friday nights and Steel Bowl clashes with Farrell still define the twin-city calendar.
Evidence: Farrell Steelers boys basketball built a District 10 reputation nicknamed for the mill town. Context: gym rivalries with Sharon pack the same shared labor market that filled the mills.

tagline.en: Sharon harmony on the national charts

history.en: Tony Butala, born in Sharon in 1940, founded The Lettermen — close-harmony hits like The Way You Look Tonight and When I Fall in Love. He later opened a Vocal Group Hall of Fame in his hometown to honor ensembles from doo-wop to Motown, and fought for years to keep that dream on State Street and the Columbia Theatre.

Raised in Mercer — the county seat east of the Shenango mill towns — Reznor graduated Mercer High in 1983 after jazz band, marching band, and musical theater. He left Allegheny College for Cleveland and built Nine Inch Nails. Same county as Buhl Park; different town. Frame him as Mercer County orbit, not a Sharon childhood claim.

tagline.en: Free music at the Performing Arts Center

history.en: Frank Buhl put a bandstand in the original farm. Today free Wednesday and Sunday concerts fill the Performing Arts Center — community bands, tributes, and Buhl Day on Labor Day. Steel endowment still buys summer nights under the trees.
Immigrant steel culture needed singing clubs. Sharon's Apollo Maennerchor survives with Festhalle concerts while most valley ethnic clubs faded. Blues, rock, and German programs still share the room.

WPIC signed on in 1938. 1950s Sharpsville record hops at Angel's Casino rode DJ promotion from the station. In 1960 Johnny and Martha Krizancic founded Marjon Records in the Sharon–Hermitage area — hundreds of polka, tamburitza, and local country/garage sides. Downtown Rockin' on the River continues the outdoor habit.

Menagerie formed in Hermitage in the Blood, Sweat & Tears vein — horns, funk, and hard rock for valley youth when live music was central. They ran Club Menagerie and a boutique; reunion shows decades later still drew thousands of locals who remembered the peak mill-town nightlife.

Evidence: Local press (Business Journal Daily; Tribune Chronicle / Vindicator) dates Cedars Lounge as a downtown Youngstown rock venue from 1975 at 23 North Hazel Street (Gallagher Building) after Tommy Simon took over the family bar. Primary legacy: original local and regional bands (Infidels and peers). After a 2012 eviction, Mara Simon and Billy Danielson reopened as Cedars West End at 706 Steel Street in 2013; fifty-year lineage marked in June 2025. Context: on the same downtown corner system as the State Theater’s Tomorrow Club / Agora — after big shows on Federal, crowds finished the night at Cedars on Hazel.

tagline.en: Muddy Waters · Outlaws · The Godz · Spyro Gyra

history.en: Evidence: The State Theater at 213 West Federal Street ran as Tomorrow Club, Youngstown Agora (31 Dec 1978–23 July 1982), then Star Theatre / later names; demolished 2008 (facade retained). Blues/jazz: Muddy Waters at Tomorrow Club 25 June 1978 and Agora 9 March 1980; Spyro Gyra at Star Theatre 20 October 1985. Southern rock: the Outlaws at Tomorrow Club three times (1976–77) and again at Star Theatre. Ohio hard rock: rock-tour databases list The Godz — Columbus “biker metal,” often called Ohio’s rock ’n’ roll machines — at Tomorrow, Youngstown, on 21 May 1978 (same hall; also documented at Cleveland Agora). Cedars sat a block away at 23 North Hazel.

George Jig Warren and Gary Moe Meszaros opened in a vacant auto service station in March 1974 — cook-your-own steak first, then wings that put Sharon on the national map. Bike Night and the original Chestnut Street address still matter.

Evidence: Official site tonyspizzaandpub.com places Tony's Pizza & Pub at 628 Stambaugh Avenue, Sharon, PA 16146 (724-347-3323), serving the Shenango Valley with pizza, sandwiches, wings, and a casual pub — and claims over 70 years as one of America's older pizza shops. Context: after the mills, Sharon neighborhood counters kept the valley table going; this pin is Sharon, not Hermitage.
East State Street neighborhood pizza that has fed the valley for generations — the kind of counter where everyone already knows your order.

Context & etiquette: New Wilmington / Volant Old Order roads are a living settlement since about 1847. Slow for buggies, buy when stands are open, leave people out of photos. The map pin is geography — not an invitation to trespass.

Evidence: Frank Buhl insisted activities stay free so working people could bring families. The trust, donations, and community partners still fund golf, concerts, and trails on roughly 270 acres. Context: the atlas hub remains here because the valley still meets here.

history.en: Context: Youngstown sits roughly sixty miles from both Cleveland and Pittsburgh and about fifteen to twenty minutes from Sharon–Farrell. The Shenango and Mahoning valleys were one labor market — mills, leagues, nightlife, and contested rackets followed the same map.

Context: Historians note Youngstown was too small for a resident Cosa Nostra family, so Cleveland and Pittsburgh split — then fought over — local gambling, vending, and related rackets. That structural fact explains why the Valley saw repeated turf wars instead of one stable “home” outfit.

Context: In March 1963 the Saturday Evening Post published John Kobler’s “Crime Town U.S.A.,” citing a decade of bombings and killings and open hobnobbing between officials and racketeers. Treat the nickname as period journalism — then ask what later courts and FBI files proved.

Evidence (public history): Locals called the numbers or policy game “the bug.” Mid-century bombing wars over bug territories helped earn Youngstown the “Bomb Town” reputation before the 1970s climax. Cash from mill paydays fed the underground economy — Context for why the stakes stayed high.

Evidence: Through the mid-1970s the Valley remained split — Cleveland interests tied to the Carabbia brothers versus Pittsburgh interests around Jimmy Prato with Joey Naples and Lenny Strollo. After Scalish’s 1976 death, published histories describe a Youngstown faction war peaking about 1978–1981. Same decade: Black Monday at Sheet & Tube.

Evidence: On 6 October 1977 Irish labor figure Danny Greene was killed by car bomb in Cleveland. Ronald “Ronnie the Crab” Carabbia of the Youngstown–Struthers Cleveland faction was among those convicted in connection with that murder. The Cleveland family’s late-1970s civil war weakened its hold; Youngstown’s balance of power shifted in those same years.

Evidence: Charles “Charlie the Crab” Carabbia disappeared in December 1980 after being lured to a meeting; his car was later found in Cleveland. In 1990s federal proceedings, Lenny Strollo testified that Prato and Naples ordered the killing to cement Pittsburgh control of Youngstown, and that he placed the summoning call. That testimony is court Evidence — museum reading states what was sworn, not street legend.

Context: Black Monday — 19 September 1977 — Youngstown Sheet & Tube closed Campbell Works (~5,000 jobs). Within about five years ~50,000 Mahoning Valley jobs disappeared. Organized crime did not cause deindustrialization, but rackets and mill-town decline share one map and one decade.

Evidence: The violent 1970s climax left Pittsburgh dominant into the Naples–Strollo years. A major late-1990s FBI investigation produced dozens of indictments; Strollo cooperated and testified. That cleanup is the legal coda — the gallery’s center of gravity remains the 1970s war that decided who ran the Valley.

Scholastic rules: Context = geography and press reputation. Evidence = contemporary reporting, FBI affidavits entered in public hearings, and sworn court testimony. Do not romanticize bombings. Do not invent private addresses. Neighboring Shenango towns appear because the border is porous — not because every mill worker was involved.
